<role>
You are articraft. Turn the user's request into a realistic 3D object or
assembly in the run workspace. `main.py` is the required entry point, but you may
create other Python files when they make the model or its checks clearer.

The object should read clearly from its shape, named geometry, and construction.
Its motion should read clearly when motion is part of the design. This is a
visual modeling workflow. Do not claim structural safety,
manufacturing tolerances, compliance, print readiness, or real world fit unless
the request asks for it and the checks prove it.
</role>

<quality_requirements>
Four requirements guide every design choice.

1. REALISTIC GEOMETRY. Use real world dimensions and believable proportions.
   Treat build123d and the public mesh helpers as complementary authoring
   choices. Prefer build123d when exact boundaries, constant wall thickness,
   openings, bores, rims, mating faces, or local fillets matter. Use the mesh
   library for freeform surfaces whose form is best described by profiles,
   lathes, lofts, or sweeps. A field based weld rebuilds every input surface on
   its sampling grid, so do not use it across a precise surface only to soften
   one local joint. Research plausible approaches before you choose or combine
   them. Familiarity and implementation speed are not reasons to use primitive
   solids when another public helper would capture the visible form better.
   Mesh usage is not a goal by itself. Model hollow bodies, openings, frames,
   rails, brackets, hinge barrels, shafts, controls, and other visible
   construction when the real object needs them. Tessellate curved surfaces
   finely enough to read smooth rather than faceted.
2. INTENTIONAL MOTION. Model independent motion when the request, a reference,
   or the ordinary construction of the object clearly requires it. Use the
   matching joint freedoms and plausible motion limits. A removable part may be
   a separate seated body. Do not invent a hinge, slide, latch, or other retained
   mechanism for a part that is normally lifted away.
3. INTENTIONAL CONNECTIONS. Every separate piece of geometry within one rigid
   body must connect to that body. Overlap within one rigid body is free and
   counts as connected, so attach a protrusion by extending its OWN end a few
   millimeters into the surface it meets. A retained rigid body needs real
   support or a real constraint. A deliberately removable rigid body may instead
   rest against a mating surface in the authored pose. Never add a separate
   piece whose only job is to close a gap. Use an explicit test allowance only
   when separation is a real part of the requested design.
4. NO UNINTENDED OVERLAPS. Keep distinct bodies separate when the design calls for
   separation. Small local overlap is acceptable for a captured pin, seated
   insert, nested part, or compressed interface. Give each intentional case a
   precise test allowance and a check that proves the intended relationship.

Compile checks and authored checks are design evidence. Use them to inspect and
repair the model. Never remove, cap, fuse, or simplify prompt-critical visible
geometry only to make a check pass.
</quality_requirements>

<workflow>
Start with the SDK quickstart that is already in the conversation. Before the
first edit, read the current `main.py` and the SDK references needed for the
design. For a simple object, read only the closest geometry reference and
example unless a specific question remains. Consider plausible build123d and
mesh approaches when the representation is not clear. In that case, do not stop
at the first workable API. Read enough to understand the relevant signatures,
coordinate rules, and limits. Use parallel `read` calls when comparing
independent references.

When a relevant SDK page names a reference figure, use `view_image` if the
figure can clarify the geometry, construction order, or visible result. Do not
load unrelated gallery images. Inspect independent images in one parallel group.

Make a compact internal brief before editing. Set the object scale, root part,
part relationships, visible construction, intended overlaps, and checks. Include
moving parts and support paths when the design has them. Include the geometry
strategy for each major visible form and why it fits. Use conservative real
world dimensions when the request gives no size.

Add a validation brief before editing. Name the shape measurements that should
hold and any contacts or clearances that should stay valid. Add mechanism poses
only when the design has independent motion.
Choose the broad views and close views that will show the result clearly. Name
any selected part, section, or motion view needed to judge
internal construction or movement. Every validation brief must include at least
one overall model view. An object with independent motion must also include a
view that shows its important motion. Add a close view only when an opening,
rim, joint, or curved transition cannot be judged in the overall view.

Build a complete first version, then write `previews.py`. Import `object_model`
from `main` and use the public `render_view(...)` function. Render every view
named in the validation brief. Run the script with
`"$ARTICRAFT_PYTHON" previews.py` through `exec_command`.

Open each useful preview with `view_image` before the first compile. Calling the
renderer is not visual inspection. Check the silhouette, proportions, part
transitions, repeated features, supports, clearances, and important mechanism
poses. Add or revise geometry when a preview shows a crude primitive substitute,
a missing secondary form, a weak connection, or unclear motion.

Register the final useful preview files with `attach_artifact(...)` in
`run_tests()`. The compiler does not render or copy images.
Registered images remain in the workspace, and their safe paths appear in the
returned `<compile_signals>` block.

Run `compile` after the first complete version. Repair the named defect. If the
same defect repeats, use one short `exec_command` inspection before another small
edit.

A successful compile does not replace visual inspection. If compile feedback or
an edit changes the model, run `previews.py` again and inspect every affected
image before the next compile. Finish only when the current workspace compiles,
the current preview images have been inspected, and the four quality
requirements are met.
Finish only when the current workspace compiles and the four quality requirements
are met.
</workflow>

<authoring_contract>
`main.py` must define `build_object_model()`, `object_model`, and `run_tests()`.
`object_model` must be a `articraft.sdk.RigidBodyAssembly`. `run_tests()`
must return a `articraft.sdk.TestReport`.

Import build123d authoring names from `build123d`. Import public assembly, mesh,
joint, and testing names from `articraft.sdk`. Choose imports after
you choose the geometry strategy. Do not import private SDK modules, the larger
Articraft package, viewer code, storage code, or data libraries.

The public SDK is a starting point, not a limit on the code you may write. When
it lacks an operation, create a small local module such as
`geometry_helpers.py` or `analysis.py`. Local modules may use the public SDK,
build123d, NumPy, trimesh, Pillow, and the Python standard library. Keep one-off
object logic local. Do not modify the installed SDK during a run.

Keep exact and freeform work separate when that preserves quality. A rigid body may
contain both build123d shapes and mesh shapes. For a mesh shell, derive matching
inner and outer sections from the same frames so their boundaries and wall
thickness stay aligned. Make through cutters cross their target surface
cleanly. Do not rely on nearly tangent or coincident booleans.

Create geometry through rigid bodies. The exact API is:

```python
model = RigidBodyAssembly("object_name")
base = model.rigid_body("base")
base.add(shape, name="body", material=Material.STEEL)
```

`RigidBody.add` accepts a build123d shape or a public mesh geometry value. The `name`
argument is required and must be unique within the body. Say what each shape is
made of with `material=Material.STEEL` (or `ALUMINUM`, `ABS_PLASTIC`, `GLASS`,
`HARDWOOD`, `RUBBER`): one word settles the shape's mass, its behavior on
contact, and how it looks. Different shapes on one body may be different
materials. Use `coating=Material.RUBBER` when the outside is a different
material from the inside -- a rubber grip on a steel bar is heavy like steel and
grippy like rubber. Add `color=` to tint one shape. For anything more, derive a
variant with `Material.STEEL.but(roughness=0.75)` and give it a name to reuse.
Build a new one only when the library has nothing close: `Material(name="ceramic",
density=2400.0)`. Never encode material semantics in the shape name.
Use `body.shape(name)` when a named shape is needed later. Do not invent a
`GeometryElement` API, and do not pass geometry to `model.rigid_body(...)`.

Motion is two steps. `body.at(...)` binds a point or a build123d `Location`,
`Plane`, `Axis`, face, edge, or vertex to that body. Prefer geometry features:
they survive dimension changes and avoid copied coordinate arithmetic.
The feature's natural axis becomes frame-local Z: an axis direction, a flat
face's normal, a straight edge's tangent, or a round feature's axis of
symmetry (a cylindrical face or hole rim anchors the hinge that spins about it).
`model.joint(name, body0.at(...), body1.at(...), dofs=...)` connects two bound
frames. No `JointDOF` is fixed, one rotational axis is a hinge, one linear axis
is a slide, and three rotational axes are a ball. Then
`model.articulation(root=..., joints=[...])` names the spanning tree the
simulator solves. Use `model.frame_in(frame, other_body)` when the same physical
frame must be expressed on another body, especially for loop closures. Use the
exact signatures in the current SDK docs. Do not use build123d joints to
describe articraft motion.

Count the pivots before writing joints. A body pinned in two places takes two
joints, and that makes the mechanism a ring rather than a chain -- linkages,
four-bars, parallel grippers, scissor mechanisms and folding braces all are.
Author every joint the mechanism physically has, then leave the ring-closing one
out of the articulation. Authoring a ring as a chain is a modelling error: the
bodies export and then flap loose under simulation.

The two bound frames of a joint coincide at rest. All linear values are meters.
Use radians for explicit `JointFrame.rpy` and rotational limits, and make every
limit range contain zero, because zero is the pose you authored. Build123d
locations keep build123d's degree convention and are converted exactly by
`body.at(...)`. Use the same meter scale for build123d coordinates, mesh helper
inputs, prismatic travel, and test distances.
</authoring_contract>

<testing>
Use `TestContext(object_model)` and return `ctx.report()`. Add a small set of
prompt-specific checks for the important shape, support relationship, contact,
clearance, or intended overlap. Add mechanism and pose checks when independent
motion is part of the design. Record useful dimensions and mesh measurements as
metrics. Use a blocking threshold only for an explicit requirement or a clear
defect. Sample important joints through their motion instead of checking only
the rest pose. Track a point when its path makes the motion easier to verify.

Create visual files in `previews.py` with `render_view(...)`. Register the final
useful PNG files with `attach_artifact()`. You may also create and register a
custom JSON, CSV, or text file. Write custom numeric checks when a public helper
cannot express an important property. Working previews may remain unregistered
in the workspace.
You may create and register a custom JSON, CSV, or text file. Write custom
numeric checks when a public helper cannot express an important property.

Compile owns model validity, the single root rule, mesh health, USDZ validation,
and USDZ readback. Mesh health covers bad triangles, invalid edges, disconnected
solid debris, winding, and orientation. Its overlap, isolation, disconnected
geometry, scale, and motion findings are nonblocking diagnostics. Decide which
findings matter for the requested object and add precise authored checks for
them.

Do not weaken a check only because it reports a real defect. First decide whether
the representation, geometry, articulation, pose, or named check is wrong. Scope
intentional overlap and isolation allowances to the exact reported relationship
and give a concrete reason. Use `allow_mesh_issues(...)` only when the exact
issue on the exact named shape is intentional. Never use it to hide accidental
holes, bad triangles, or debris.
</testing>

<tools>
The available tools are `read`, `edit`, `write`, `exec_command`, `write_stdin`,
and `compile`.

Use `read` for workspace text files, SDK docs, examples, and snippets. The SDK
reference pages are the source for public signatures, defaults, coordinate rules,
and failure cases. Do not spend shell calls guessing the API.
The `view_image` tool is also available for relevant workspace images and SDK
reference figures.
Use `edit` for one or more exact replacements in one file and `write` for an
intentional whole file replacement. Put disjoint replacements for the same file
in one `edit` call. The tool matches every replacement against the original
file. Use these tools for `main.py` and for local helper modules. Use
`exec_command` and `write_stdin` for local inspection scripts, short geometry
inspections, and debugging tasks that `read` and `compile` do not cover. Python
commands can import the public SDK. Use `"$ARTICRAFT_PYTHON"` to run them
with the same interpreter as articraft. Run `compile` after an actual file
change and before the final response.

`read` calls may run in parallel. Treat shell calls and all workspace changes
as ordered actions.
`view_image` calls may also run in parallel.
</tools>

<final_response>
After the latest workspace compiles successfully, return a visible final response
in one or two short sentences. State what you built. Name the main motion only
when independent motion is part of the design. Do not include the full script.
</final_response>

<sdk_quickstart>
This SDK quickstart is preloaded for the run. Use it as the first reference. Before writing code, inspect the current script and survey the relevant SDK pages across plausible build123d and mesh approaches. Use parallel reads and image views when comparing independent references. Do not stop at the first workable API.

# SDK quickstart

Use meters for lengths and radians for angles. Build123d rotations are the only exception.
They use degrees.

A `RigidBody` contains named shapes that always move together. A shape can be a
`build123d.Shape` or `MeshGeometry`.

Apply a build123d location before you add the shape. The SDK does not apply a second shape
transform.

```python
from build123d import Box, Pos

from articraft.sdk import RigidBodyAssembly, TestContext, TestReport

model = RigidBodyAssembly("small_table")
body = model.rigid_body("body")
top = body.add(Box(0.8, 0.5, 0.04), name="top", color=(0.45, 0.24, 0.10))
body.add(Pos(X=0.36, Y=0.21, Z=-0.36) * Box(0.04, 0.04, 0.7), name="leg_1")

object_model = model


def run_tests() -> TestReport:
    ctx = TestContext(object_model)
    return ctx.report()
```

Give each shape a unique name within its body. A color contains RGB or RGBA values from zero
through one.

Make connected shapes overlap within one rigid body. For example, extend a leg into the table
top by a few millimeters.

Use build123d for exact boundaries, wall thickness, openings, bores, rims, and local fillets.
Use mesh helpers for freeform sections or paths.

## Decide whether the object moves

Many objects have no independent motion. A loose teapot or saucepan lid is a separate seated
part, not a reason to invent a hinge. Add a retained mechanism only when the request,
reference, or ordinary construction calls for one.

## Add retained motion

First, use `model.joint(...)` to connect two bodies. Then use `model.articulation(...)` to
select the solver tree.

```python
from articraft.sdk import JointAxis, JointDOF

moving_model = RigidBodyAssembly("wall_cabinet")
frame = moving_model.rigid_body("cabinet_frame")
frame.add(Box(0.8, 0.08, 0.6), name="frame")
door = moving_model.rigid_body("cabinet_door")
door.add(Box(0.8, 0.02, 0.6), name="panel")

moving_model.joint(
    "door_hinge",
    frame.at((-0.4, 0.0, 0.0)),
    door.at((-0.4, 0.0, 0.0)),
    dofs=(JointDOF(JointAxis.ROT_Z, limits=(0.0, 1.9)),),
)
moving_model.articulation("main", root=frame, joints=["door_hinge"])
```

Use `body.at(...)` to bind a point or build123d feature to its body. Pass the same feature to
both endpoints when possible.

The endpoint frames coincide at rest. Each joint limit uses radians or meters and must include
zero.

Count every physical pivot. A body with two pivots needs two joints, which creates a closed
loop.

Author every joint in a closed loop. Omit one closing joint from the articulation tree.

## Read the applicable reference

Read only the reference that applies to your next task:

- Read `docs/sdk/common/10_errors.md` for errors and validation.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/20_core_types.md` for shared units and types.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/30_assembly.md` for assemblies, bodies, and shapes.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/35_joints.md` for joints and articulations.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/37_materials.md` for materials and mass.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/38_simulation_settings.md` for gravity and initial motion.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/40_testing.md` for checks and geometry inspection.
- Visual views and report artifacts: `docs/sdk/common/45_visual_evidence.md`.
- Read `docs/sdk/common/50_usdz_export.md` for USDZ output.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/00_mesh_geometry.md` for mesh editing and solid builders.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/10_profiles.md` for profiles and curve samples.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/20_wires_and_sweeps.md` for wires, pipes, and sweeps.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/30_section_lofts.md` for section lofts and guide paths.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/40_booleans_and_shells.md` for booleans, shells, and welds.
- Read `docs/sdk/mesh/50_refinement_and_smoothing.md` for mesh refinement.

The detailed build123d pages are under `docs/sdk/build123d/`. Their examples use arbitrary
dimensions, so convert all dimensions to meters.

Read only the example that is closest to your task:

- `docs/sdk/examples/hollow_shell.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/section_loft_with_wires.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/mixed_articulated_assembly.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/molded_mug.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/mass_properties.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/closed_loop_linkage.py`
- `docs/sdk/examples/variable_sweep_and_loft.py`

Run `compile` after meaningful changes. Use failed checks to improve the design. Do not remove
geometry that the prompt requires.
</sdk_quickstart>

<task>
User request:

Recreate the chest of drawers shown in the reference photo. It is a white painted wooden dresser about 1.2 m wide, 0.45 m deep and 0.9 m tall, with nine drawers in a three-by-three grid, standing on four short feet. Each drawer is a box that slides straight out of the front of the carcass on its own horizontal prismatic joint, so the model has nine prismatic joints, one per drawer. Each drawer front is fluted with fine vertical grooves, carries one small brass bar handle at its centre that stands proud of the front face, and has a brass bracket at each corner. The carcass has two side panels, a top, a bottom, a back, two vertical dividers and horizontal rails, so that every drawer sits in its own opening. Z is up and the drawer fronts face +Y.

Edit `main.py` in the run workspace and build the requested object. Meet the four
quality requirements from the system prompt. Use realistic geometry, model only
the motion the design requires, support retained parts, seat removable parts,
and avoid unintended overlap.

Start with the preloaded SDK quickstart. Before choosing a representation, use
`read` to survey the relevant SDK references and compare plausible build123d and
mesh approaches. Do not stop at the first workable API. Research enough to form
an internal geometry strategy for the major visible forms. Then implement the
object with `RigidBody.add(shape, name=..., material=...)` for known physical surfaces
or `color=...` for plain matte ones, add prompt-specific checks, and run `compile`.

Treat every compile signal as design evidence. Preserve prompt-critical visible
geometry while you repair named defects.
After a successful compile, review the visual representation separately and
improve any major form that uses a crude substitute when a public authoring
method would fit it better.
Then return a short visible summary of the object. Include its main motion only
when independent motion is part of the design.
</task>

L383: ## Exact collision and distance checks
L384: 
L385: Every method in this section records one check and returns true on pass or false on failure. The
L386: optional `name` replaces the generated check name.
L387: 
L388: ### `expect_no_collision(part_a, part_b, *, shape_a=None, shape_b=None, name=None)`
L389: 
L390: Passes when the selected triangle meshes do not collide. This is a direct collision test. It does
L391: not use the compiler's meaningful overlap thresholds.
L392: 
L393: ### `expect_collision(part_a, part_b, *, shape_a=None, shape_b=None, name=None)`
L394: 
L395: Passes when at least one selected shape pair collides. If several pairs collide, the report uses a
L396: representative pair with the largest bounds overlap.
L397: 
L398: ### `expect_contact(part_a, part_b, *, shape_a=None, shape_b=None, contact_tol=1e-6, name=None)`
L399: 
L400: Passes when the selected geometry collides or its minimum distance is at most `contact_tol`.
L401: `contact_tol` must be nonnegative and uses meters.
L402: 
L403: ### `expect_distance(part_a, part_b, *, shape_a=None, shape_b=None, min_distance=0.0, max_distance=None, name=None)`
L404: 
L405: Passes when the minimum mesh distance is at least `min_distance` and no more than
L406: `max_distance`, when an upper bound is provided. Both bounds are inclusive and nonnegative. A
L407: collision has distance zero. An upper bound below the lower bound records a failed check.
L408: 
L409: Shape selectors are independent for these methods. For example, `shape_a="shaft"` can be checked
L410: against every shape in `part_b`.
L411: 
L412: ## Exact bounds checks
L413: 
L414: These checks use world axis aligned bounds. They do not prove mesh contact or mesh collision.
L415: 
L416: ### `expect_gap(positive_part, negative_part, *, axis, positive_shape=None, negative_shape=None, min_gap=None, max_gap=None, max_penetration=None, name=None)`
L417: 
L418: The signed gap is:
L419: 
L420: ```text
L421: positive bounds minimum on axis minus negative bounds maximum on axis
L422: ```
L423: 
L424: `axis` must be `"x"`, `"y"`, or `"z"`. A positive result is a gap. A negative result is bounds
L425: penetration.
L426: 
L427: When `min_gap` is omitted, the lower bound is zero. If `max_penetration` is provided, the lower
L428: bound is `-max_penetration`. A provided `min_gap` takes precedence. `max_gap` is an optional
L429: inclusive upper bound. An upper bound below the lower bound records a failed check.
L430: 
L431: ### `expect_within(inner_part, outer_part, *, inner_shape=None, outer_shape=None, axes="xy", margin=0.0, name=None)`
L432: 
L433: Passes when the inner bounds stay inside the outer bounds on every requested axis. `margin`
L434: allows the inner bounds to extend that far beyond the outer bounds and must be nonnegative.
L435: 
L436: ### `expect_overlap(part_a, part_b, *, shape_a=None, shape_b=None, axes="xy", min_overlap=0.0, name=None)`
L437: 
L438: Passes when the projected bounds overlap by at least `min_overlap` on every requested axis. A
L439: minimum of zero allows exact bounds contact. `min_overlap` must be nonnegative.
L440: 
L441: For `axes`, use a string such as `"xy"` or a sequence such as `("x", "z")`. Repeated axes are
L442: ignored. At least one axis is required.
L443: 
L444: `expect_overlap()` proves projected overlap only. It does not declare an allowance and does not
L445: suppress the compiler's mesh overlap check.
L446: 
L447: ## Allowances
L448: 
L449: Allowances describe intentional exceptions to compiler owned physical checks. Each reason must be
L450: nonempty.
L451: 
L452: ### `allow_overlap(part_a, part_b, *, reason, shape_a, shape_b)`
L453: 
L454: Both shape names are required. The allowance covers only that exact named shape
L455: pair.
L456: 
L457: ```python
L458: ctx.allow_overlap(
L459:     "shaft",
L460:     "hub",
L461:     shape_a="steel_shaft",
L462:     shape_b="bore_liner",
L463:     reason="The shaft is captured inside the bearing liner.",
L464: )
L465: ```
L466: 
L467: An allowance does not hide another collision between the same two parts.
L468: 
L469: An overlap allowance affects only `fail_if_parts_overlap_in_current_pose()`, including the copy of
L470: that check which the compiler runs. It does not make `expect_no_collision()` or another authored
L471: check pass.
L472: 
L473: Pair an allowance with an exact check that explains the intended relationship. For a captured
L474: shaft, an `expect_contact()`, `expect_within()`, or bounds gap check can provide that evidence.
L475: 
L476: ### `allow_isolated_part(part, *, reason)`
L477: 
L478: Allows one named part in `fail_if_isolated_parts()`. If several touching parts form one floating
L479: group, every part in that group must have an allowance. The check still records a nonblocking
L480: warning that the group was allowed.
L481: 
L482: An isolation allowance does not affect disconnected shapes inside one rigid part.
L483: 
L484: ### `allow_mesh_issues(part, *, shape, issues, reason)`
L485: 
L486: Allows exact mesh health issue types on one named shape. It does not hide other issue types on the
L487: same shape or any issue on another shape.
L488: 
L489: ```python
L490: ctx.allow_mesh_issues(
L491:     "shade",
L492:     shape="fabric_panel",
L493:     issues=(MeshHealthIssue.BOUNDARY_EDGES,),
L494:     reason="This named fabric panel is an intentional open surface.",
L495: )
L496: ```
L497: 
L498: Use this only for a shape that is meant to have the reported property. Repair accidental holes,
L499: bad triangles, disconnected debris, and invalid topology.
L500: 
L501: ## Compiler owned checks
L502: 
L503: The compile worker runs `run_tests()` first. It then copies authored overlap, isolation, and mesh
L504: health allowances into a new context and runs these baseline checks before export:
L505: 
L506: 1. `check_model_valid()`
L507: 2. `fail_if_mesh_unhealthy()`
L508: 3. `fail_if_parts_have_no_mass()` (only while the physics lane is enabled)
L509: 4. `fail_if_isolated_parts()`
L510: 5. `warn_if_part_contains_disconnected_geometry_islands()`
L511: 6. `warn_if_absurd_dimensions()`
L512: 7. `fail_if_parts_overlap_in_current_pose()`
L513: 8. `fail_if_articulation_separates_child()`
L514: 
L515: If model validity fails, the worker stops the rest of the baseline pass. When the object is valid
L516: enough to inspect, model validity, mesh health, missing mass properties, and USDZ validation can
L517: block the compiler. The other baseline methods appear as nonblocking diagnostics.
L518: Add an authored check when one of those findings is important to the requested object.
L519: The failed check still makes the compile fail and prevents final publication.
L520: 
L521: The merged report keeps one copy of each check name. A compiler failure replaces an authored
L522: failure with the same name. A passing compiler check never erases an authored failure. Exact
L523: duplicate failures, warnings, and allowance strings are also merged.
L524: 
L525: ### Model validity and root policy
L526: 
L527: `check_model_valid()` calls `object_model.validate()`. The assembly must contain valid named
L528: geometry and one connected physical joint graph.
L529: 
L530: Each articulation validates its root and selected tree. An assembly with several articulations
L531: does not have one global root.
L532: 
L533: ### Physical isolation
L534: 
L535: `fail_if_isolated_parts(*, contact_tol=1e-6, name=None)` builds a physical contact graph at the
L536: current pose. Two parts are connected when their meshes collide or their minimum distance is no
L537: more than `contact_tol`. An articulation by itself does not count as physical support.
L538: 
L539: The graph starts at the root part from the articulation tree. A physically separate group fails
L540: unless every part in that group has an isolation allowance. Parent and child parts are checked in
L541: the same way as any other pair.
L542: 
L543: ### Disconnected geometry within a part
L544: 
L545: `warn_if_part_contains_disconnected_geometry_islands(*, contact_tol=1e-6, name=None)` splits all
L546: named shapes into mesh components. Components are connected when they collide or are within the
L547: contact tolerance. The compiler records a warning when one rigid part contains more than one
L548: physical group.
L549: 
L550: Disconnected geometry is nonblocking in the baseline pass. Use the blocking form when one of your
L551: design requirements needs it:
L552: 
L553: ```python
L554: ctx.fail_if_part_contains_disconnected_geometry_islands(contact_tol=1e-6)
L555: ```
L556: 
L557: Nested closed solids with positive volume intersection count as connected geometry.
L558: 
L559: ### Scale warnings
L560: 
L561: `warn_if_absurd_dimensions(*, max_dimension=1000.0, outlier_ratio=100.0, name=None)` checks the
L562: largest world bounds span of every named shape. It warns when a shape is larger than
L563: `max_dimension` meters. It also warns when a shape is more than
L564: `outlier_ratio` times the median positive shape span.
L565: 
L566: This check is always nonblocking.
L567: 
L568: ### Meaningful overlap
L569: 
L570: `fail_if_parts_overlap_in_current_pose(*, overlap_tol=0.005, overlap_volume_tol=5e-7, name=None)`
L571: checks every named shape pair from different parts at the current pose, including adjacent parent
L572: and child parts.
L573: 
L574: A pair can be a blocking overlap only when all of these facts are true:
L575: 
L576: 1. Its world bounds overlap by more than `overlap_tol` on all three axes.
L577: 2. Its bounds overlap volume is greater than `overlap_volume_tol` cubic meters.
L578: 3. The triangle meshes collide.
L579: 4. No matching overlap allowance exists.
L580: 
L581: For watertight meshes, a pair blocks only when its intersection volume exceeds
L582: `overlap_volume_tol`.
L583: 
L584: Without solid volume, the pair blocks for penetration greater than `1e-6` meters. It also blocks
L585: when no penetration depth is available.
L586: 
L587: Mere contact passes. Bounds penetration at or below either physical threshold also passes. A
L588: shape allowance suppresses only its exact pair. The report includes at most one representative
L589: unallowed shape pair for each part pair, chosen by overlap depth and volume.
L590: 
L591: The baseline check uses the rest pose. Use `with ctx.pose(...)` and an authored exact check when a
L592: different pose is important to the requested mechanism.
L593: 
L594: ## Choose checks
L595: 
L596: Checks are design evidence. Do not delete or simplify visible geometry only to make a check pass.
L597: 
L598: Use shape names when a part contains unrelated regions. Use a small number of checks that prove
L599: the important support, clearance, insertion, or motion. If a check finds a real defect, repair the
L600: geometry, articulation, pose, or exact selector. Add an allowance only when the physical
L601: relationship is intentional."}}

L3: Render images after the model can run. The renderer does not need a window or graphics
L4: processor.

L6: It writes PNG files that you can inspect with `view_image`.

L19:     SectionView,
L20:     TestArtifact,
L21:     annotate_image,
L22:     render_view,
L23: )
L24: ```
L25: 
L26: ## Mark a reference image
L27: 
L28: `ImagePoint` stores one normalized image coordinate. `Reticle` gives the point a label and
L29: display color.
L30: 
L31: Use `annotate_image` to draw reticles on a reference image. The workspace stores the
L32: prepared input as `reference.png`, `reference.jpg`, or `reference.webp`.
L33: 
L34: The `u` coordinate increases to the right. The `v` coordinate increases down the image.
L35: 
L36: ```python
L37: annotate_image(
L38:     "reference.png",
L39:     (
L40:         Reticle(ImagePoint(0.18, 0.52), "handle root"),
L41:         Reticle(ImagePoint(0.82, 0.34), "tip"),
L42:     ),
L43:     "qa/previews/reference-markers.png",
L44: )
L45: ```
L46: 
L47: Open the output with `view_image`. Confirm that each reticle marks the intended feature.
L48: 
L49: A reticle records visible evidence. It cannot find depth from one image.
L50: 
L51: ## Preview before compilation
L52: 
L53: Create `previews.py` after you have the first complete model. Import `object_model` from
L54: `main.py` and call the public renderer.
L55: 
L56: ```python
L57: from main import object_model
L58: from articraft.sdk import ModelView, SectionView, render_view
L59: 
L60: 
L61: def main() -> None:
L62:     render_view(
L63:         object_model,
L64:         ModelView.three_quarter(
L65:             selected_parts=("housing", "service_door"),
L66:             show_joints=True,
L67:         ),
L68:         "qa/previews/assembly.png",
L69:     )
L70:     render_view(
L71:         object_model,
L72:         SectionView(
L73:             plane_origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
L74:             plane_normal=(0.0, 1.0, 0.0),
L75:         ),
L76:         "qa/previews/section.png",
L77:     )
L78: 
L79: 
L80: if __name__ == "__main__":
L81:     main()
L82: ```
L83: 
L84: Run the script with the Articraft Python interpreter:
L85: 
L86: ```sh
L87: "$ARTICRAFT_PYTHON" previews.py
L88: ```
L89: 
L90: `ARTICRAFT_PYTHON` points to the interpreter that runs Articraft. You do not need private
L91: imports or SDK changes.
L92: 
L93: Open each useful output with `view_image`. Calling the renderer is not visual inspection.
L94: 
L95: Working previews can stay under `qa/previews/`. Attach a preview when it is useful final
L96: evidence:
L97: 
L98: ```python
L99: ctx.attach_artifact(
L100:     "qa/previews/section.png",
L101:     name="housing section",
L102:     caption="The section shows the shell, bore, and internal support.",
L103: )

L105:     "qa/clearance_samples.json",
L106:     name="clearance samples",
L107:     caption="Clearance at each tested joint pose.",
L108: )
L109: ```
L110: 
L111: The path must be relative to the run workspace. `TestArtifact` supports these file types:
L112: 
L113: - PNG, JPEG, and WebP images.
L114: - JSON and CSV data.
L115: - Markdown and plain text.
L116: 
L117: ## Understand compilation behavior
L118: 
L119: The compiler does not render or copy images. Registered files stay in the workspace.
L120: 
L121: The `compile` tool returns safe workspace paths for registered images. It does not attach image
L122: content.
L123: 
L124: Open each useful path with `view_image`.
L125: 
L126: ## Render a model view
L127: 
L128: `ModelView` renders visible triangles with a depth buffer:
L129: 
L130: ```python
L131: ModelView(
L132:     direction=(1.0, -1.0, 0.7),
L133:     up=(0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
L134:     projection="orthographic",
L135:     width=640,
L136:     height=480,
L137:     color_by="part",
L138:     show_bounds=False,
L139:     show_joints=False,
L140:     selected_parts=(),
L141:     selected_shapes=(),
L142:     points=(),
L143:     lines=(),
L144: )
L145: ```
L146: 
L147: Use `ModelView.front()`, `side()`, `top()`, or `three_quarter()` for a common camera.
L148: 
L149: `projection` accepts `orthographic` or `perspective`. `color_by` accepts `part`, `shape`, or
L150: `material`.
L151: 
L152: Use `selected_parts` or `selected_shapes` to isolate geometry. Use `PointOverlay` for a world
L153: position and `LineOverlay` for a world segment.
L154: 
L155: ```python
L156: tip_path = ctx.track_point("arm", (0.0, 0.0, 0.4), poses)
L157: view = ModelView.side(
L158:     points=tuple(
L159:         PointOverlay(point, label=f"sample {index}")
L160:         for index, point in enumerate(tip_path)
L161:     ),
L162:     lines=tuple(
L163:         LineOverlay(tip_path[index], tip_path[index + 1])
L164:         for index in range(len(tip_path) - 1)
L165:     ),
L166: )
L167: ```
L168: 
L169: ## Render a section
L170: 
L171: `SectionView` intersects selected triangles with one plane:
L172: 
L173: ```python
L174: SectionView(
L175:     plane_origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
L176:     plane_normal=(0.0, 1.0, 0.0),
L177:     horizontal=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0),
L178:     vertical=(0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
L179: )
L180: ```
L181: 
L182: The horizontal and vertical vectors must be in the section plane. Omit them when exact
L183: directions are not necessary.
L184: 
L185: Use `MeridionalSectionView` for a form around one axis:
L186: 
L187: ```python
L188: MeridionalSectionView(
L189:     axis=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0),
L190:     radial_direction=(0.0, 0.0, 1.0),
L191:     origin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
L192: )
L193: ```
L194: 
L195: The axis and radial direction must be perpendicular.
L196: 
L197: ## Render a motion strip
L198: 
L199: `MotionStripView` puts several poses in one image:
L200: 
L201: ```python
L202: MotionStripView(
L203:     articulation="door_hinge",
L204:     positions=(0.0, 0.6, 1.2),
L205:     view=ModelView.side(width=320, height=280, show_joints=True),
L206: )
L207: ```
L208: 
L209: Set `dof` when the joint has several degrees of freedom. It accepts an axis name or the
L210: qualified DOF identifier:
L211: 
L212: ```python
L213: MotionStripView(
L214:     articulation="removable_lid",
L215:     dof="removable_lid.transZ",
L216:     positions=(0.0, 0.04, 0.10),
L217:     view=ModelView.side(width=320, height=280),
L218: )
L219: ```
L220: 
L221: Omit `positions` to sample the authored motion limits. A continuous joint uses a half turn.
L222: 
L223: ## Render directly
L224: 
L225: Call `render_view` from local preview code. You do not need a test report.
L226: 
L227: ```python
L228: render_view(
L229:     object_model,
L230:     ModelView.three_quarter(),
L231:     "qa/three_quarter.png",
L232:     pose={"door_hinge": 0.8},
L233: )
L234: ```
L235: 
L236: `render_view(...)` accepts `ModelView`, `SectionView`, `MeridionalSectionView`, or
L237: `MotionStripView`. The output file must be PNG."}}

L390: ## LatheGeometry
L391: 
L392: ```python
L393: LatheGeometry(
L394:     profile: Iterable[tuple[float, float]],
L395:     *,
L396:     segments: int = 32,
L397:     closed: bool = True,
L398:     angle: float = 2 * pi,
L399:     start_angle: float = 0.0,
L400:     axis: str = "z",
L401:     cap_ends: bool = True,
L402: )
L403: ```
L404: 
L405: Each profile point is `(radius, z)`. The helper revolves the profile around the
L406: selected axis. `axis` can be `"x"`, `"y"`, or `"z"`. Radius values must be
L407: nonnegative. Segments are clamped to at least 3.
L408: 
L409: `angle` must be greater than zero and at most a full turn. `start_angle`
L410: rotates the first section around the selected axis. A partial revolution of a
L411: closed profile gets flat end caps when `cap_ends=True`. Partial end caps require
L412: a closed profile.
L413: 
L414: With `closed=True`, the profile must contain at least three distinct points and
L415: must enclose a nonzero area in the radius and Z plane. The helper closes the
L416: profile before revolving it. With `closed=False`, the profile needs at least
L417: two distinct points and produces an open surface.
L418: 
L419: Use `from_shell_profiles(...)` for a thin revolved shell.
L420: 
L421: ```python
L422: LatheGeometry.from_shell_profiles(
L423:     outer_profile: Iterable[tuple[float, float]],
L424:     inner_profile: Iterable[tuple[float, float]],
L425:     *,
L426:     segments: int = 32,
L427:     start_cap: str = "flat",
L428:     end_cap: str = "flat",
L429:     lip_samples: int = 6,
L430: ) -> LatheGeometry
L431: ```
L432: 
L433: The outer and inner profiles each need at least two points. Their authored
L434: order defines the start and end. Cap modes are `"flat"` and `"round"`.
L435: `lip_samples` controls the curved connector used by a round cap and is clamped
L436: to at least 2.
L437: 
L438: A round cap needs at least one endpoint with a positive radius. It cannot connect two points
L439: on the rotation axis because that would create a ring of collapsed faces. Use a flat cap when
L440: both endpoints lie on the axis.
L441: 
L442: ```python
L443: cup = LatheGeometry.from_shell_profiles(
L444:     outer_profile=[(0.045, 0.0), (0.050, 0.09)],
L445:     inner_profile=[(0.040, 0.004), (0.044, 0.085)],
L446:     end_cap="round",
L447:     segments=48,
L448: )
L449: ```

L451: ## LoftGeometry
L452: 
L453: ```python
L454: LoftGeometry(
L455:     profiles: Iterable[Iterable[tuple[float, float, float]]],
L456:     *,
L457:     cap: bool = True,
L458:     closed: bool = True,
L459:     interpolation: str = "linear",
L460:     samples_per_span: int = 1,
L461:     close_path: bool = False,
L462:     parameterization: str = "uniform",
L463:     tension: float = 0.0,
L464:     cap_style: str = "flat",
L465:     cap_segments: int = 6,
L466:     cap_length: float | None = None,
L467: )
L468: ```
L469: 
L470: This is the direct mesh loft. Use `section_loft(...)` when sections have
L471: different point counts, need path offsets, need symmetry, or need repair.
L472: 
L473: Use `from_shell_profiles(...)` for a hollow loft with open ends and a solid wall:
L474: 
L475: ```python
L476: LoftGeometry.from_shell_profiles(
L477:     outer_profiles: Iterable[Iterable[tuple[float, float, float]]],
L478:     inner_profiles: Iterable[Iterable[tuple[float, float, float]]],
L479:     *,
L480:     interpolation: str = "linear",
L481:     samples_per_span: int = 1,
L482:     parameterization: str = "uniform",
L483:     tension: float = 0.0,
L484: ) -> LoftGeometry
L485: ```
L486: 
L487: The outer and inner inputs must have the same section count and point count. Corresponding
L488: points should describe the same position around each section. The helper builds both wall
L489: surfaces and joins them with an annular face at each end. It does not use a mesh boolean.
L490: 
L491: ```python
L492: spout = LoftGeometry.from_shell_profiles(
L493:     outer_profiles=[outer_root, outer_middle, outer_tip],
L494:     inner_profiles=[inner_root, inner_middle, inner_tip],
L495:     interpolation="catmull_rom",
L496:     samples_per_span=3,
L497:     parameterization="centripetal",
L498: )
L499: ```
L500: 
L501: At least two profiles are required. Every profile must have the same point
L502: count. With `closed=True`, each profile needs at least three distinct points
L503: and must enclose a nonzero planar area. Adjacent profile centers must be
L504: different. The helper compares adjacent profiles and corrects reversed loop winding.
L505: Corresponding points must still describe the same feature around each profile.
L506: 
L507: With `closed=False`, profiles are treated as open polylines with at least two
L508: points. Only adjacent points are connected. Caps are only added when both
L509: `cap` and `closed` are true. Use planar first and last profiles when you need
L510: reliable caps.
L511: 
L512: `interpolation="linear"` connects the authored profiles directly. Set
L513: `interpolation="catmull_rom"` to fit a smooth path through corresponding
L514: profile points. `samples_per_span` controls how many rings the helper creates
L515: from one authored profile to the next. It must be at least one. Smooth
L516: interpolation needs a value greater than one to add a visible curve between
L517: authored profiles.
L518: 
L519: Smooth interpolation passes through every authored profile. It can extend
L520: outside the straight span when profile size or position changes sharply. Add
L521: another authored profile or use linear interpolation when the surface must
L522: stay within a strict boundary.
L523: 
L524: For Catmull Rom spans, `parameterization` can be `"uniform"`, `"chord"`, or
L525: `"centripetal"`. Chord and centripetal modes account for the distance between
L526: profile centers. Centripetal mode is a good starting point when the profile
L527: spacing is uneven. `tension` ranges from `0.0` to `1.0` and reduces tangent
L528: strength as it increases.
L529: 
L530: The default `cap_style="flat"` triangulates each end profile. `"round"` grows
L531: smaller rings toward a rounded tip. `cap_segments` controls the number of rings.
L532: `cap_length` sets the distance from the end profile to the tip. When it is
L533: omitted, the loft uses the largest profile radius at that end.
L534: 
L535: With `close_path=True`, the helper connects the final profile back to the first
L536: profile and does not add caps. A closed path needs at least three profiles.
L537: This supports ring forms whose profile changes around a complete loop.
L538: 
L539: ```python
L540: loft = LoftGeometry(
L541:     profiles=[
L542:         [(-0.05, -0.04, 0.0), (0.05, -0.04, 0.0), (0.05, 0.04, 0.0), (-0.05, 0.04, 0.0)],
L543:         [(-0.03, -0.02, 0.12), (0.03, -0.02, 0.12), (0.03, 0.02, 0.12), (-0.03, 0.02, 0.12)],
L544:     ],
L545:     interpolation="catmull_rom",
L546:     samples_per_span=6,
L547:     parameterization="centripetal",
L548:     tension=0.1,
L549:     cap_style="round",
L550:     cap_segments=8,
L551:     cap_length=0.015,
L552: )
L553: ```
L554: 
L555: ## ExtrudeGeometry
L556: 
L557: ```python
L558: ExtrudeGeometry(
L559:     profile: Iterable[tuple[float, float]],
L560:     height: float,
L561:     *,
L562:     cap: bool = True,
L563:     center: bool = True,
L564:     closed: bool = True,
L565: )
L566: 
L567: ExtrudeGeometry.centered(
L568:     profile,
L569:     height,
L570:     *,
L571:     cap: bool = True,
L572:     closed: bool = True,
L573: ) -> ExtrudeGeometry
L574: 
L575: ExtrudeGeometry.from_z0(
L576:     profile,
L577:     height,
L578:     *,
L579:     cap: bool = True,
L580:     closed: bool = True,
L581: ) -> ExtrudeGeometry
L582: ```
L583: 
L584: The profile is a two dimensional loop in XY. Height must be positive. A
L585: centered extrusion spans `-height / 2` through `height / 2`. With
L586: `center=False`, or with `from_z0(...)`, it spans `0` through `height`.
L587: 
L588: The helper accepts either clockwise or counterclockwise profile input and
L589: normalizes it. The profile must contain at least three distinct points and
L590: must have nonzero area. Caps are only added when both `cap` and `closed` are
L591: true. With `closed=False`, the last profile point is not connected back to the
L592: first, so the result is an open strip.
L593: 
L594: ## ExtrudeWithHolesGeometry
L595: 
L596: ```python
L597: ExtrudeWithHolesGeometry(
L598:     outer_profile: Iterable[tuple[float, float]],
L599:     hole_profiles: Iterable[Iterable[tuple[float, float]]],
L600:     height: float,
L601:     *,
L602:     cap: bool = True,
L603:     center: bool = True,
L604:     closed: bool = True,
L605: )
L606: ```
L607: 
L608: The outer loop and every hole loop are in XY. Each loop needs at least three
L609: distinct points and nonzero area. The helper normalizes loop winding. For a
L610: capped solid, every hole must lie inside the outer loop and the profiles must
L611: be valid simple polygons. Manifold performs the cap triangulation.

L613: Height and centering follow `ExtrudeGeometry`. If `hole_profiles` is empty, the
L614: helper delegates to `ExtrudeGeometry`.

L623: )
L624: ```
